top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) credits a mature body of work that pairs an explanatory framework, the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium and task-based labour demand, with transparent local-labour-market designs for import competition. Replication, cross-country extension and sustained critique over one to three decades have qualified the magnitude and persistence of the effects but not their existence. I treat it as one question with two channels: how exposure to technology and trade shifts labour demand and who bears the adjustment costs. Katz's wage-structure and skill-premium line is distinct from his education-technology work with Goldin, so a citation about labour demand, wages and local adjustment can include him without restating the 2023 prize. The costs are real. Dorn is excluded only by the three-name cap, and Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu sit outside the credited set. P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is a defensible narrower alternative and my second choice, because it gives cleaner credit for a trade-shock-centred discovery but drops the framework that explains why the shocks matter for wages. I rank P000 last because both configurations meet the common criteria of achievement, maturity and attribution well enough to award.
recusal_note: No co-authorship, institutional or collaborator tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my profile. My field, labour economics and the economics of crime, is close to B006 in subject matter, and I have tried to apply the common criteria without extra weight for that proximity. I presented the 2023 Goldin prize announcement, which is a role and not a connection to a candidate, and Katz's best-known work with Goldin bears on his marginal credit. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
